China arrests and detains residents who have fled North Korea for survival 
and subsequently repatriates them to North Korea. 

Such forced repatriation is carried out on the premise of 
a systematic operational structure and the intent and awareness of the actors, 
and it constitutes a clear illegal act under international law.

 

 

 

 

 

 

8,360 cases of forced repatriation are recorded 
in the "NKDB Unified Human Rights Database." 

This signifies that forced repatriation has continued from the 1960 repatriation (E11-B-0070), collected as the first occurrence, until the present day.

 

 

 

 

 

[How Forced Repatriation is Carried Out: 
A Systematized Operational Structure] 

 

 

Chinese public security agencies lead the crackdown and arrest of North Korean escapees in China. In detention, they investigate identities, movement routes, and the circumstances of the border crossing, after which they decide whether to repatriate and hand the individuals over to subsequent enforcement agencies along with related documents.

 

Afterward, forced repatriation is executed by the Public Security Border Defense Corps. Once the border is crossed, the North Korean State Security Agency takes custody, conducts additional investigations, and temporarily detains the individuals in collection centers.

 

Subsequently, the North Korean Security Department and the courts proceed with investigation, preliminary examination, sentencing, and adjudication. The subjects then undergo imprisonment in Labor Training Camps, prisons, and political prison camps.

 

 Even after their release, those who fled North Korea are subject to continuous post-release surveillance by the State Security Agency and the Security Department.

 

 

 

 

 

[Changes in the System Around 2018: 
Establishment of the China National Immigration Administration]

 

 

Forced repatriation is not a measure based on the arbitrary judgment of certain agencies or individual officials, but is the result of an organized and planned administrative procedure based on the Chinese Party and administrative system.

 

In particular, this process was reorganized into a more unified command system following the establishment of the National Immigration Administration in 2018.

 

Previously, various levels of public security agencies under the State Council's Ministry of Public Security initiated the crackdown and repatriation of escapees in China. These actions were executed by the Public Security Border Defense Corps (under the People's Armed Police Force), which received political guidance from the Central Military Commission and administrative direction from the Exit-Entry Administration Bureau and the Border Control Department of the Ministry of Public Security.

 

However, in 2018, the Bureau of Exit and Entry Administration, the Border Control Department, and the Public Security Border Defense Corps were integrated into a single entity: the National Immigration Administration (NIA). Following this merger, the forced repatriation of escapees in China transitioned into a structure operated systematically under a unified and centralized government administrative command.

 

 

 

 

 

[Why is it Illegal?: 
China's Responsibility for the Forced Repatriation of Escapees in China]

 

 

In that the forced repatriation of escapees in China is being carried out organizationally and systematically by Chinese government agencies, it can be evaluated as an act attributable to the state rather than a deviation by individual officials, and accordingly, China's state responsibility can be established.

 

Furthermore, these actions suggest the possibility of falling under "crimes against humanity" as defined by the Rome Statute, moving beyond the scope previously discussed as violations of the Refugee Convention and the Convention Against Torture.

 

 

 

The forced repatriation of escapees in China can be evaluated as an "attack against any civilian population," a core constituent element of crimes against humanity, in that it is a forced movement carried out coercively across international borders against civilians residing legally.

 

In particular, these acts are being carried out collectively under the widespread and systematic operation of Chinese government agencies, and the illegality is further strengthened by the fact that substantial remedies or procedural rights were not sufficiently guaranteed during the repatriation decision process.
 

 

 

Additionally, the fact that the individuals are exposed to serious human rights violations as a result of forced repatriation is also an important factor in the judgment.

 

Furthermore, it appears that the Chinese government agencies executing the forced repatriation were fully aware that the escapees had established a de facto legal status within certain regions through marriage or other means, and that they would likely face persecution and serious human rights violations upon repatriation.

 

Nevertheless, it is confirmed through numerous testimonies that the expulsion was carried out with the awareness and intent to forcibly move them abroad, which can be evaluated as an act that satisfies the subjective and objective constituent elements of the "crime of deportation" among the crimes against humanity under the Rome Statute.

 

 

 

 

 

The journey toward a home 
that should be a place of longing 
is instead transformed into a devastating tragedy.

Testimonies from detainees

 

 

Legal execution

“When I was at the Provincial MSS,

I heard that a certain woman had been executed by the MSS

for passing Workers’ Party newspapers to China

and selling election lists for money.”

E10-I-6885 (Detained in 2008)

 

 

Death due to unknown causes

“I was arrested by the Provincial MSS 

for drug smuggling and taken in.

Once inside, I ended up revealing various things 

during interrogation.

After that… (omitted) I think he died

in the Provincial MSS detention cell in 2013.”

E14-I-0596 (Detained in 2013)

 

 

Illegal Detention

“When I was in the waiting room in 2018,

everyone who had been brought in there

had been arrested for superstitious actions.”

E22-I-0150 (Detained in 2018)

 

 

Torture/ violations with physical dimensions

“On the first day of the interrogation,

they told me to hand over 

my South Korean passport.

When I said, ‘How could I possibly have a passport?’

they cursed at me, grabbed a book, 

and beat me with it.

When they beat me, of course I got hit.”

E24-I-1313 (Detained in 2017)

 

 

Disappearance

“There was a North Korean man 

who had been arrested.

He was from Rimyongsu District,

and I saw him briefly at the MSS.

Then, after being at the MSS, 

he was taken away within two or three days,

and after that there was no contact from him.

Even his family said they did not know what happened to him.”

E16-I-1149 (Detained in 2014)

 

 

Internal exile (forced exile)

“After being released from the MSS, we were expelled.

They took away our house and everything.

My whole family was expelled together to Pungsan.”

E14-I-4392 (Expelled in 2010)

 

 

Forced abortion

“She was repatriated while pregnant at the age of 18. 

That was in 2005.

She was taken into the MSS, where they beat her,

and even though she was pregnant, 

they forcibly aborted the baby

while cursing at her and saying 

that there was no need

for her to give birth if it was a Chinese child.

They injected a thick syringe 

into her waist to carry out the abortion.”

E25-I-0590 (Detained in 2005)

 

 

Extortion

“I do not even know how much money was spent

trying to save my older sister.

An MSS Instructor said he would save her,

so we gave him 3 million South Korean won,

and when things went wrong again, 

we sent another 20,000 yuan.”

E16-I-0367 (Experienced in 2014)

 

 

Denial of the right to adequate food

“At the MSS, they gave us corn.

And they gave us dried radish greens soaked 

in salty yellowish water.

It was the kind of food that ordinary rural households

would be glad to feed to pigs.”

E15-I-3598 (Detained in 2013)

Testimonies from detainees

 

 

Sexual violations
“When I arrived at the Musan County MSS, 
there were two women in a room 
with men present. In front of the men, 
they made us take off all our clothes, 
made us repeatedly squat and stand (pompu), 
put on plastic gloves, examined our uterus, 
and spread open our anus. 
Two men sat at a desk, 
taking notes and watching. 
I truly cannot describe the humiliation 
I felt at that time.” 
E12-I-6231 (Detained in 2003)

 

 

Illegal Detention
“It was June 2009. I had crossed into China, 
was caught by the PSBDC, 
and around the 24th was sent across 
through the Nampyeong customs office 
and transferred to the Musan County MSS.” 

E10-I-0536 (Detained in 2009)

 

 

Torture/ violations with physical dimensions
“When I was interrogated, 
I was taken to a solitary confinement cell, 
where there was one instructor’s desk. 
I sat facing him, answered questions, 
and wrote self-criticism statements. 
Leather gloves… why would he put on leather gloves 
while I was just sitting there? 
He made me kneel and beat me. 
Anyway, I was taken out every day.” 
E10-I-12050 (Detained in 2006)

 

 

Failure to provide health care facilities and personnel
“When I arrived at the Musan County MSS, 
I was so thirsty that I drank 
any water I could find. 
At that time, I developed severe colitis. 
I kept having a fever and other symptoms.” 
E10-I-6653 (Detained in 2004)

 

 

Looting / Theft by government agent
“When you enter the MSS, 
they conduct naked body searches on everyone, 
men and women alike. 
At that time, they took the Chinese yuan 
I had hidden under the soles of my shoes. 
They tell you to speak honestly, 
but who would honestly say that? 
So I said I did not know, 
but when they peeled it open, it came out. 
They are experts in that kind of thing.” 
E25-I-0396 (Detained in 2002)

 

 

Extortion
“In 2009, I helped an elderly woman I knew 
cross into China and was caught by the MSS. 
The MSS Director told them to forgive me, 
but the MSS informants made things difficult for me. 
I was harassed so much that I brought 
100,000 North Korean won, Chinese liquor, 
one chicken, and ten eggs to the office.” 
E15-I-0510 (Experienced in 2009)

 

 

Lay-off or dismissal/ demotion
“In May 2009, a prisoner of war from the ROK Army 
was sent across to China. 
To be precise, I only assisted, 
and it was done by the company MSS Instructor. 
But that instructor was arrested, 
and I was also summoned. 
Since it was not something I had done, 
I was discharged on the charge of 
facilitating illegal border crossing.” 
E13-I-1938 (Discharged in 2010)

 

 

Denial of the right to fair trial and hearing
“At the MSS, they told me 
to admit that I was a spy. 
They told me to write a self-criticism statement 
saying that I had tried to help China and South Korea. 
It was to establish the achievement 
that they had caught a spy in Musan. 
I was there until August 24, 2009.” 
E15-I-0145 (Detained in 2008)

 

 

Forfeiture of property
“At the Musan County MSS, 
they confiscated 800 yuan in Chinese money from me 
and gave me 800 yuan in counterfeit money. 
My watch was also confiscated.” 
E12-I-1468 (Detained in 2006)

 

 

Denial of the right to adequate food
“They did give us three meals a day, 
but it was about one spoonful each time, 
and in winter they gave us cold rice with cold soup. 
When they gave us noodles, 
they just floated broken pieces of noodles in water.” 
E12-I-2195 (Detained in 2006)

 

 

Denial of the right to adequate medical services
“When I was being handled at the Musan County MSS, 
they said I would live if I wrote honestly, 
so I wrote honestly on a piece of paper. 
Then I tried to hide it by tearing it up and eating it. 
At that time, swallowing the paper 
caused me to become sick. 
I developed colitis and other illnesses, 
and my blood pressure dropped. 
They told me to come out, 
saying they would treat me, 
but they made me lie down on the floor 
and kicked me with their boots.” 
E10-I-3834 (Detained in 2006)

 

 

Denial of the right to adequate accommodation
“The Musan County MSS detention facility 
had no heating, and it was cold 
because there was only a thin blanket. 
There was no pillow and nothing else.” 
E11-I-6688 (Detained in 2004)

 

 

Involuntary forced labor
“It seems that farms and construction sites 
receive instructions like that from the MSS, 
asking them to provide work using criminals. 
Then they take us out and make us work. 
When we went to farms, 
we worked with corn, soybean powder, picked peppers, 
and when we were sent to construction sites, 
we worked at construction sites.” 
E24-I-1614 (Detained in 2007)

Testimonies from detainees

 

 

Sexual violations

“That is what they do when you enter the MSS. 

They conduct naked body searches.

I remember being shocked the first time, 

when they put on gloves

and inserted their hands down below to search me.”

E23-I-0444 (Detained in 2011)

 

 

Illegal Detention

“I was at the Shinuiju MSS for about 40 days. 

Normally it was 20 days,

but Ebola had broken out at that time. 

They said people coming in from abroad

had to be quarantined, 

so I stayed 20 more days, for a total of 40 days.”

E25-I-0508 (Detained in 2015)

 

 

Torture / violations with physical dimensions

“At the Shinuiju MSS, they beat me severely 

with something like firewood.

On some days, they called me 

in more than three or four times,

and each time they beat me

and slammed my head against the wall.”

E11-I-11571 (Detained in 2003)

 

 

Denial of reasonable visitation rights

“When I was taken into the MSS, 

my father came to the MSS bringing food for me,

but the MSS Instructor in charge reportedly said 

he did not know anyone like that.

Once you enter the MSS, 

you are completely cut off from the outside.”

E14-I-4869 (Detained in 1998)

 

 

Forfeiture of property

“At the Shinuiju MSS, I paid 100 yuan in Chinese money,

but after deducting the cost of necessary items such as soap,

they gave me 3,500 North Korean won 

when I left for the Police Holding Camp.

They simply took 500 yuan in Chinese money from me.”

E14-I-0076 (Detained in 2009)

 

 

Denial of the right to adequate food

“At the MSS, they gave us only a few kernels of whole corn, 

not even one hundred kernels.

They just served whole corn on a small spoon into a dish.

The soup was not even salty soup; 

it was just something watery.”

Illegal Detention

“I was at the Shinuiju MSS for about 40 days.
